revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Best Deal on Juice Boxes
revealWordProblem.text: The Chef Academy snack bar sells juice boxes in two pack sizes: a 4-pack for $6.00 and a 6-pack for $8.10. Which pack size is the better deal, and how do you know? Explain your reasoning using unit rates.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Find the unit rate (cost per juice box) for each pack. The 4-pack: $6.00 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per juice box. The 6-pack: $8.10 ÷ 6 = $1.35 per juice box. Since $1.35 is less than $1.50, the 6-pack is the better deal.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 3.4–3.7: 3.4 Equivalent Ratios, 3.5 Compare Ratios, 3.6 Use Ratio Reasoning, 3.7 Ratio and Rate Problem Solving. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 3.4–3.7
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 3.4: Multiply or divide both numbers by the same amount to make an equivalent ratio. • 3.5: Compare ratios fairly by making one part equal or by finding the unit rate. • 3.6: Find the scale factor, then multiply both parts; cross-multiply to check a proportion. • 3.7: Find the unit rate by dividing, then multiply it to find the amount you need.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 3.4 — Equivalent Ratios: Multiply or divide both numbers by the same amount to make an equivalent ratio.
Lesson 3.5 — Compare Ratios: Compare ratios fairly by making one part equal or by finding the unit rate.
Lesson 3.6 — Use Ratio Reasoning: Find the scale factor, then multiply both parts; cross-multiply to check a proportion.
Lesson 3.7 — Ratio and Rate Problem Solving: Find the unit rate by dividing, then multiply it to find the amount you need.

youDo.title: Show you're caught up
lines: The practice below mixes problems from Lessons 3.4–3.7. Each problem is tagged with its lesson number.
Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

discourse.prompt: How does the ratio table help you find the price for ANY number of pounds? What is the unit rate, and where does it show up in your table?
discourse.sentenceFrame: The unit rate is ___ per pound because 18 ÷ 3 = ___; I can multiply the unit rate by ___ to find the cost of any amount.

explore.instructions: Team 1 knows that 3 pounds of chicken cost $18. Complete the ratio table to find the cost for different amounts, then determine the unit rate.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.4) Chef Montoya's dressing uses 3 spoons of oil to 4 spoons of vinegar (3:4). Which recipe card shows an EQUIVALENT ratio?
optional.explanation: Multiply both parts of 3:4 by 3: 3 x 3 = 9 and 4 x 3 = 12, so 9:12 is equivalent to 3:4.
choiceFeedback: Scale both numbers by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.5) Chef Academy's snack bar sells 3 mini quiches for $6 or 5 mini quiches for $8. Which is the better deal per quiche?
optional.explanation: 3 for $6 is $6 / 3 = $2.00 per quiche. 5 for $8 is $8 / 5 = $1.60 per quiche. $1.60 < $2.00, so 5 quiches for $8 is the better deal.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.6) Chef Reyes's pasta dough uses 2 eggs for every 3 cups of flour. For a banquet, the kitchen mixes 9 cups of flour. How many eggs are needed to keep the same ratio?
optional.explanation: Scale factor: 9 cups divided by 3 cups = 3. Multiply the eggs by the same factor: 2 x 3 = 6 eggs.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.7) In the kitchen, 3 pizzas feed exactly 12 people. At the same rate, how many pizzas are needed to feed 20 people?
optional.explanation: First find the unit rate: 12 people ÷ 3 pizzas = 4 people per pizza. Then 20 people ÷ 4 people per pizza = 5 pizzas.
choiceFeedback: Re-check how many times you need to multiply or scale.

approaching.explanation: Multiply both parts by 2: 2×2 = 4 and 5×2 = 10, so 4:10 is equivalent to 2:5.
choiceFeedback: Scale both numbers by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.
hints: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying BOTH parts of 2:5 by the same number.
For each choice, ask: what did the 2 become, and what did the 5 become? Both must be multiplied by the same amount.
Try multiplying both parts of 2:5 by 2 and see what ratio appears. Then look for that pattern among the choices.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.4) A recipe uses 4 eggs for every 6 cups of flour. Which ratio is equivalent?
approaching.explanation: Divide both by 2: 4÷2 = 2 and 6÷2 = 3. The ratio 2:3 is equivalent to 4:6.
choiceFeedback: Scale both numbers by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.
hints: You can scale a ratio DOWN too — divide both parts by the same number.
Look for a number that divides evenly into both 4 and 6, then divide each part by it.
Both 4 and 6 are even, so divide each by 2 and see what simpler ratio you get.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.5) Chef A uses 2 cups of cheese for every 8 crackers. Chef B uses 3 cups of cheese for every 9 crackers. Who uses more cheese per cracker?
approaching.explanation: Chef A: 2÷8 = 0.25 cups per cracker. Chef B: 3÷9 ≈ 0.33 cups per cracker. Chef B uses more cheese per cracker.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: You can't compare 2 cups and 3 cups directly — the chefs use different numbers of crackers.
Find each chef's cheese for ONE cracker: divide cheese by crackers for each, then compare the two rates.
Chef A: divide 2 ÷ 8. Chef B: divide 3 ÷ 9. Compare those two decimals to see who uses more per cracker.

approaching.explanation: Convert to the same denominator: 3:4 = 6:8. Since 6:8 > 5:8, the ratio 3:4 is greater.
choiceFeedback: Compare the ratios carefully — which one is greater?
hints: The second numbers (4 and 8) don't match, so the ratios aren't ready to compare yet.
Rewrite the ratios with the same second number — 8 works nicely, since 4 × 2 = 8 — then compare the first numbers.
Scale 3:4 by 2: multiply both parts to get an out-of-8 ratio. Then compare its first number with the 5 in 5:8.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.6) A recipe uses 4 cups of broth for every 10 servings. How many cups of broth are needed for 30 servings?
approaching.explanation: Scale factor: 30 ÷ 10 = 3. Multiply broth by 3: 4 × 3 = 12 cups.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: The servings jumped from 10 to 30 — the broth must grow by the same factor.
Find the scale factor by dividing the new servings by the recipe's servings, then multiply the broth by it.
Divide 30 ÷ 10 to get the scale factor — then multiply 4 cups of broth by that number.

approaching.explanation: Divide 6:9 by 3 to get 2:3. Since both ratios simplify to 2:3, they are equivalent.
choiceFeedback: Scale both numbers by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.
Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: Two ratios are equivalent when one simplifies (or scales) exactly into the other.
Try dividing both parts of 6:9 by the same number — adding or subtracting the parts proves nothing about ratios.
Divide the 6 by 3 and the 9 by 3, then compare what you get with 2:3.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.7) A bakery makes 24 cookies in 3 batches. What is the unit rate of cookies per batch?
approaching.explanation: Unit rate: 24 cookies ÷ 3 batches = 8 cookies per batch.
choiceFeedback: Re-check how many times you need to multiply or scale.
hints: 'Per batch' means the number of cookies in exactly ONE batch.
Divide the total cookies by the number of batches to find one batch's share.
Divide 24 cookies by 3 batches — the quotient is your cookies per batch.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.7) Apples cost $5 for 4 pounds. What is the cost per pound?
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: 'Cost per pound' asks for the dollars for exactly ONE pound.
Divide the total price by the number of pounds. Keep the money on top: dollars ÷ pounds.
Divide 5 ÷ 4 — writing it as 5.00 ÷ 4 can make the decimal easier to see.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.4) Marcus earns $45 for every 3 hours of work. How much does he earn in 8 hours?
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: 8 hours is not a whole-number multiple of 3 hours, so find what Marcus earns in ONE hour first.
Unit rate: divide the $45 by the 3 hours, then multiply that hourly pay by 8 hours.
Divide 45 ÷ 3 to get dollars per hour — then multiply that rate by 8.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 3.4) Spot the Common Mistake — Simplifying a Ratio

workedExample.label: Set up the ratio
workedExample.work: A student wants to write 12:18 in simplest form.

workedExample.label: Find the common factor
workedExample.work: Both 12 and 18 can be divided by 6.

onLevel.correctWork: Divide BOTH parts by the same number: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 12:18 simplifies to 2:3.
hints: Look at Step 3. They divided 12 by 6 but divided 18 by 3 — those are different numbers.
To keep ratios equivalent, divide both numbers by the SAME amount. 12:18 divided by 6 each gives 2:3.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.5) Store A sells 3 mangoes for $6. Store B sells 5 mangoes for $9. Which store offers a better price per mango?
onLevel.explanation: Store A: $6÷3 = $2.00 per mango. Store B: $9÷5 = $1.80 per mango. Store B has the better (lower) price per mango.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: The stores sell different counts for different prices — compare the price of ONE mango.
Divide dollars by mangoes for each store, then choose the store with the lower per-mango price.
Store A: divide 6 ÷ 3 for its price per mango. Store B: divide 9 ÷ 5. Compare the two prices.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 3.5) onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: Compare Chef Reyes's dressing (4 tbsp oil : 6 tbsp vinegar) to Chef Tran's dressing (5 tbsp oil : 8 tbsp vinegar). Which dressing is oilier?

workedExample.label: Scale each ratio
workedExample.work: Chef Reyes: 6 × 4 = 24, so oil = 4 × 4 = 16, giving 16:24. Chef Tran: to reach 24 he also multiplies by 4: oil = 5 × 4 = 20, giving 20:24.

workedExample.label: Conclusion
workedExample.work: Since 20 > 16, Chef Tran's dressing is oilier.

onLevel.correctWork: Each ratio needs its own multiplier to reach 24 — Chef Reyes and Chef Tran do not use the same multiplier. Chef Tran's vinegar is 8, and 8 × 3 = 24 (not 8 × 4 = 32), so multiply BOTH parts of his ratio by 3, not 4: oil = 5 × 3 = 15, giving 15:24. Now compare with equal vinegar (24): Chef Reyes has 16 tbsp oil and Chef Tran has 15 tbsp oil. Since 16 > 15, Chef Reyes's dressing is actually oilier.
hints: Look at Step 3. Each ratio needs its own multiplier to reach the common denominator (24) — Chef Reyes and Chef Tran do not need the same multiplier.
8 × 3 = 24, so what should you multiply BOTH parts of Chef Tran's ratio by?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.6) A chef uses the proportion 3/7 = x/28 to scale a recipe. What is x?
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: Look at the bottoms of the fractions first: the 7 became 28.
Divide 28 by 7 to find the scale factor, then multiply the top number 3 by that same factor.
Compute 28 ÷ 7, then multiply 3 by the result to get x.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 3.6) Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Set up the proportion
workedExample.work: A recipe uses 4 cups of sugar for every 9 cups of flour: 4/9 = x/27.

onLevel.correctWork: Multiply by the scale factor instead of adding it: 4 × 3 = 12 cups of sugar. To keep ratios equivalent you multiply both parts by the scale factor — you never add it.
hints: Look at Step 3. The scale factor of 3 is correct, but what operation should you use with it?
To scale a ratio you MULTIPLY both parts by the factor (4 × 3), you do not add (4 + 3).

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.7) A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. A bus travels 200 miles in 5 hours. Which vehicle is faster?
onLevel.explanation: Car: 150÷3 = 50 mph. Bus: 200÷5 = 40 mph. The car travels faster at 50 mph vs. 40 mph.
choiceFeedback: Check if this ratio is equivalent or answers what the question asks.
hints: You can't compare 150 miles and 200 miles directly — the travel times are different.
Find each vehicle's speed in miles per ONE hour: divide miles by hours, then compare the two speeds.
Car: divide 150 ÷ 3. Bus: divide 200 ÷ 5. The bigger miles-per-hour value belongs to the faster vehicle.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 3.7) onLevel — Spot the Smoothie Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: A smoothie stand makes 18 smoothies in 6 minutes. How many smoothies can it make in 10 minutes at the same rate?

onLevel.correctWork: The unit rate was divided in the wrong order. The question asks for smoothies, so find smoothies per minute: 18 smoothies ÷ 6 minutes = 3 smoothies per minute. Then 3 × 10 = 30 smoothies in 10 minutes.
hints: Look at Step 2. The question asks how many smoothies, so the unit rate should be smoothies per minute, not minutes per smoothie.
Divide 18 smoothies by 6 minutes to get 3 smoothies per minute, then multiply by 10 minutes to get 30 smoothies.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.4) Find Marcus's Mistake
hints: Look at Step 3. What operation should you use with the multiplier?
To keep ratios equivalent, you multiply both parts by the same number — not add.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.5) Find Kai's Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: Compare 3:5 and 4:7. Which ratio is greater?

workedExample.label: Scale the ratios
workedExample.work: 3:5 = 21:35 (3 × 7 = 21). For 4:7, Kai multiplies by 7 again: 4 × 7 = 28, giving 28:35.

extending.correctWork: To scale 4:7 to 35ths, multiply by 35 ÷ 7 = 5, not by 7 again: 4 × 5 = 20, so 4:7 = 20:35 (not 28:35). Now compare correctly: 21:35 vs. 20:35. Since 21 > 20, the ratio 3:5 is actually greater, not 4:7.
hints: Look at Step 3. To turn 7 into 35, Kai should multiply by 35 ÷ 7 = 5 — but he used 7 again, the denominator from the OTHER ratio.
Find the correct multiplier for 4:7 (35 ÷ 7), then multiply BOTH the 4 and the 7 by that number.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.6) Find Priya's Mistake
extending.correctWork: 5 × 4 = 20 (multiply by the scale factor, don't add it)
hints: Look at Step 3. Priya found the correct scale factor of 4, but what did she do with it?
To keep ratios equivalent, multiply both parts by the scale factor — do NOT add.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.7) Find Mia's Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: A store sells 6 oranges for $4.50. What is the cost of 10 oranges?

hints: Look at Step 3. Mia found the correct unit rate of $0.75, but what did she do with it?
To find the total cost, you multiply the unit rate by the number of items — not add.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Ratio and Rate Problem Solving is dividing in the wrong order when setting up the unit rate — for example, finding "minutes per smoothie" (6 ÷ 18) instead of "smoothies per minute" (18 ÷ 6) — or using addition instead of multiplication to scale the unit rate, like adding $0.75 + 10 instead of multiplying $0.75 × 10. Before you submit, check: does your unit rate match the units the question is asking for, and did you multiply (not add) to scale it to the new amount?

diagram.title: Runner's Pace Scales by Miles
diagram.caption: Each bar is minutes to run that many miles at 9 min per mile; the bars grow evenly, so the 5K (3.1 mi) is predicted at about 27.9 min.

connect.scenario: A runner trains for a 5K race. During practice, she runs 3 miles in 27 minutes. She wants to know her pace (minutes per mile) and predict how long the full 5K (3.1 miles) will take at the same rate.
connect.prompt: This is like our rate problem-solving work because ___ and ___ are related by ___.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 3.5) A bakery sells 4 muffins for $10 and another bakery sells 6 muffins for $14. Which bakery has the lower price per muffin?
exitTicket.explanation: First bakery: $10÷4 = $2.50 per muffin. Second bakery: $14÷6 ≈ $2.33 per muffin. The second bakery has the lower price.
choiceFeedback: Find each price per muffin and compare — recompute both.
Compare the per-muffin costs; are $10/4 and $14/6 equal?
You can compare — find each bakery's price per muffin.
hints: Compare the price of ONE muffin at each bakery, not the whole pack prices.
Divide dollars by muffins for each bakery, then pick the lower per-muffin price.
First bakery: divide 10 ÷ 4 for the price per muffin. Then divide 14 ÷ 6 and compare the two prices.
